1 Hyperparameter tuning without optimism

Two different questions: which configuration of the same model is better (tuning) and which model is better (benchmarking). The package separates the two and requires the decision criterion to be explicit — including in multi-objective cases.

Show the code 
field <- ler("field_yield")
v <- verdade$field_yield
no_out <- field[!field$plot_id %in% v$outlier_ids, ]

spec_xgb <- smf_experiment_spec(
  task = smf_task_spec("regression", "yield"),
  data = smf_data_spec("yield", c("nitrogen", "potassium", "water", "organic_matter",
                                  "block", "genotype"),
                       id_column = "plot_id", categorical = c("block", "genotype")),
  design = smf_design_spec(id_column = "plot_id"),
  preprocessing = smf_preprocess_spec("median"),
  model = smf_model_spec("boosted_tree", "xgboost",
                         parameters = list(nrounds = 60L, params = list(max_depth = 3L))),
  metrics = list(smf_metric_spec("rmse", "minimize"), smf_metric_spec("mae", "minimize")),
  reproducibility = smf_reproducibility_spec(61L)
)
space <- smf_search_space(nrounds = smf_param_int(30L, 90L),
                          params.max_depth = smf_param_int(2L, 6L))
print(space)

Four search strategies, the same space and the same budget per configuration. The pedagogical point: the search method is a budget decision, not a scientific one — and the inner resample must be identical for comparisons to make sense.

Show the code 
t_grid <- smf_tune(spec_xgb, no_out, space, smf_tuning_spec("grid", budget = 4L,
  inner_resampling = smf_resampling_spec("kfold", n_splits = 3L, seed = 61L),
  objectives = list(smf_metric_spec("rmse", "minimize")), seed = 61L))
t_rand <- smf_tune(spec_xgb, no_out, space, smf_tuning_spec("random", budget = 6L,
  inner_resampling = smf_resampling_spec("kfold", n_splits = 3L, seed = 62L),
  objectives = list(smf_metric_spec("rmse", "minimize"), smf_metric_spec("mae", "minimize")),
  decision_rule = list(type = "weighted_sum", weights = c(rmse = 0.7, mae = 0.3)),
  seed = 62L))
t_race <- smf_tune(spec_xgb, no_out, space, smf_tuning_spec("racing", budget = 6L,
  inner_resampling = smf_resampling_spec("kfold", n_splits = 4L, seed = 63L),
  objectives = list(smf_metric_spec("rmse", "minimize")), seed = 63L,
  parameters = list(min_folds = 2L)))
t_bayes <- smf_tune(spec_xgb, no_out, space, smf_tuning_spec("bayesian", budget = 6L,
  inner_resampling = smf_resampling_spec("kfold", n_splits = 3L, seed = 64L),
  objectives = list(smf_metric_spec("rmse", "minimize")), seed = 64L,
  parameters = list(initial = 3L, candidate_pool = 16L)))

method_tbl <- data.frame(
  method = c("grid", "random", "racing", "bayesian"),
  evaluations = c(nrow(t_grid@archive), nrow(t_rand@archive),
                  nrow(t_race@archive), nrow(t_bayes@archive)),
  best_rmse = c(min(t_grid@archive$rmse, na.rm = TRUE),
                min(t_rand@archive$rmse, na.rm = TRUE),
                min(t_race@archive$rmse, na.rm = TRUE),
                min(t_bayes@archive$rmse, na.rm = TRUE))
)
tab_smf(method_tbl, caption = "Four search strategies in the same space and with the same inner-fold budget.")

Show the code 
archives <- rbind(
  data.frame(method = "grid", trial = t_grid@archive$trial, rmse = t_grid@archive$rmse),
  data.frame(method = "random", trial = t_rand@archive$trial, rmse = t_rand@archive$rmse),
  data.frame(method = "racing", trial = t_race@archive$trial, rmse = t_race@archive$rmse),
  data.frame(method = "bayesian", trial = t_bayes@archive$trial, rmse = t_bayes@archive$rmse)
)
ggplot(archives, aes(trial, rmse, colour = method)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = .8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = min(archives$rmse, na.rm = TRUE), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = cores_smf[["alerta"]]) +
  facet_wrap(~method, nrow = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(grid = cores_smf[["neutro"]], random = cores_smf[["primaria"]],
                                 racing = cores_smf[["destaque"]], bayesian = cores_smf[["sucesso"]]),
                      guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "evaluation", y = "inner RMSE (kg/ha)",
       title = "Tuning archives: four search strategies")
WarningTrap

An objective that is not in spec@metrics does not produce an empty archive: it aborts with a clear error (TUNING_OBJECTIVE_NOT_IN_METRICS), listing the available metrics. This behaviour is the 1.0.2 fix for a defect that returned an empty selection in silence. The package prefers to fail loudly.

NoteInterpretation

The best inner RMSE across all methods is 287.4 kg/ha, found by racing. Inner values are not the final performance: they choose the configuration. The honest estimate of the chosen one comes from an outer resample (here, the Part 3 holdout; at the limit, nested tuning).

2 Benchmarking: comparing models with a declared criterion

The benchmark evaluates several models in the same design, with repetitions and computational cost measures. The decision comes from an explicit rule.

Show the code 
candidates <- list(
  lm = smf_model_spec("linear_regression", "stats"),
  rf = smf_model_spec("random_forest", "tidymodels",
                      parameters = list(model_engine = "ranger")),
  xgb = smf_model_spec("boosted_tree", "xgboost", parameters = list(nrounds = 60L))
)
bench <- smf_benchmark(spec_xgb, no_out, smf_benchmark_spec(
  candidates = candidates,
  metrics = list(smf_metric_spec("rmse", "minimize")),
  resampling = smf_resampling_spec("kfold", n_splits = 5L, seed = 71L),
  compute_measures = c("fit_time", "total_time"),
  repetitions = 2L, seed = 71L
))
tab_smf(bench@summary, caption = "Benchmark with 5 folds repeated twice: mean, SD, standard error and interval per candidate.")
Benchmark with 5 folds repeated twice: mean, SD, standard error and interval per candidate.
candidate metric mean sd se lower upper n
lm rmse 373.236 138.221 43.709 274.358 472.113 10
rf rmse 584.586 82.826 26.192 525.336 643.836 10
xgb rmse 497.491 75.344 23.826 443.594 551.389 10
Show the code 
dec <- smf_decide_benchmark(bench, list(type = "weighted_sum", weights = c(rmse = 1)))
tab_smf(dec, caption = "Decision by the declared rule (weight 1 for RMSE).")
Decision by the declared rule (weight 1 for RMSE).
candidate rmse .decision_score
lm 373.236 0
Show the code 
ggplot(bench@summary, aes(stats::reorder(candidate, mean), mean)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), colour = cores_smf[["primaria"]], size = .8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = fmt(mean, 0)), hjust = -0.35) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "mean RMSE (kg/ha)",
       title = "Benchmark: mean RMSE with interval") +
  ylim(0, max(bench@summary$upper) * 1.15)
NoteInterpretation

The winner by the rule is lm, with mean RMSE 373.2. The intervals overlap in part, but the conclusion does not depend on a single fold: it comes from 10 evaluations (5 folds x 2 repetitions) and from a rule declared before looking at the result.

3 Calibration: does the number mean what it promises?

A probability of 0.3 should correspond to ~30% of events. In the disease dataset, with label noise, that rarely happens without calibration. The package offers the calibrator (smf_calibrate()), the application (smf_apply_calibration()) and the report (smf_calibration_report()).

Show the code 
disease <- ler("disease_binary")
disease$disease <- factor(disease$disease, levels = c(0, 1))
set.seed(20260919)
idx <- sample.int(nrow(disease))
i_te <- idx[1:100]
i_rest <- idx[101:nrow(disease)]
i_cal <- i_rest[1:120]
i_tr <- setdiff(i_rest, i_cal)
glm_p4 <- stats::glm(disease ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4, data = disease[i_tr, ],
                     family = stats::binomial())
p_cal_tr <- stats::predict(glm_p4, disease[i_cal, ], type = "response")
p_te <- stats::predict(glm_p4, disease[i_te, ], type = "response")
P_te <- cbind(`0` = 1 - p_te, `1` = p_te)
cal_p4 <- smf_calibrate(disease$disease[i_cal],
                        cbind(`0` = 1 - p_cal_tr, `1` = p_cal_tr),
                        smf_calibration_spec("platt"))
P_te_cal <- smf_apply_calibration(cal_p4, P_te)
rel_raw <- smf_calibration_report(disease$disease[i_te], P_te, bins = 5L,
                                  positive_label = "1")
rel_cal <- smf_calibration_report(disease$disease[i_te], P_te_cal, bins = 5L,
                                  positive_label = "1")
cal_tbl <- data.frame(
  measure = c("ECE", "log loss", "Brier"),
  raw = c(rel_raw$ece, rel_raw$log_loss, rel_raw$brier),
  calibrated = c(rel_cal$ece, rel_cal$log_loss, rel_cal$brier)
)
tab_smf(cal_tbl, caption = "Same test set, same logistic regression: before and after Platt calibration (calibration partition: 120 rows).")
Same test set, same logistic regression: before and after Platt calibration (calibration partition: 120 rows).
measure raw calibrated
ECE 0.057 0.049
log loss 0.424 0.419
Brier 0.236 0.235
Show the code 
conf_raw <- rel_raw$table
conf_raw <- data.frame(predicted = conf_raw$mean_probability,
                       observed = conf_raw$observed_frequency,
                       version = "raw")
conf_cal <- rel_cal$table
conf_cal <- data.frame(predicted = conf_cal$mean_probability,
                       observed = conf_cal$observed_frequency,
                       version = "calibrated")
ggplot(rbind(conf_raw, conf_cal), aes(predicted, observed, colour = version)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  geom_line(alpha = .6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(raw = cores_smf[["neutro"]],
                                 calibrated = cores_smf[["primaria"]])) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "predicted probability (bin mean)", y = "observed frequency",
       colour = NULL,
       title = "Reliability curve: raw vs calibrated") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
ImportantInterpretation

In this partition, raw ECE is 0.0571 and calibrated ECE is 0.0486. Calibrating is not automatically better: with only 120 calibration rows, the Platt calibrator can worsen ECE — the effect depends on the partition size and on noise. The rate below measures the procedure with repetition, which is the only evidence that decides.

Show the code 
one_replicate_cal <- function(s, n_cal) {
  set.seed(s)
  n <- nrow(disease); order_idx <- sample.int(n)
  i_te_r <- order_idx[1:100]
  rest <- order_idx[101:n]
  i_cal_r <- rest[1:n_cal]
  i_tr_r <- setdiff(rest, i_cal_r)
  f <- stats::glm(disease ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4, data = disease[i_tr_r, ],
                  family = stats::binomial())
  p_c <- stats::predict(f, disease[i_cal_r, ], type = "response")
  p_t <- stats::predict(f, disease[i_te_r, ], type = "response")
  Pc <- cbind(`0` = 1 - p_c, `1` = p_c)
  Pt <- cbind(`0` = 1 - p_t, `1` = p_t)
  cr <- smf_calibrate(disease$disease[i_cal_r], Pc, smf_calibration_spec("platt"))
  Ptc <- smf_apply_calibration(cr, Pt)
  r0 <- smf_calibration_report(disease$disease[i_te_r], Pt, bins = 5L, positive_label = "1")
  r1 <- smf_calibration_report(disease$disease[i_te_r], Ptc, bins = 5L, positive_label = "1")
  c(ece_raw = r0$ece, ece_cal = r1$ece)
}
CAL_SIZE <- c(60L, 120L)
R_REP <- 40L
mc_cal <- lapply(CAL_SIZE, function(nc) {
  t(vapply(seq_len(R_REP), function(s) one_replicate_cal(s, nc), numeric(2)))
})
names(mc_cal) <- as.character(CAL_SIZE)
mc_tbl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(CAL_SIZE), function(i) {
  m <- mc_cal[[i]]
  data.frame(calibration_n = CAL_SIZE[i],
             mean_raw_ece = mean(m[, "ece_raw"]),
             mean_calibrated_ece = mean(m[, "ece_cal"]),
             improvement_rate = mean(m[, "ece_cal"] < m[, "ece_raw"]))
}))
tab_smf(mc_tbl, caption = "Platt calibration over 40 independent splits, by calibration partition size.")
Platt calibration over 40 independent splits, by calibration partition size.
calibration_n mean_raw_ece mean_calibrated_ece improvement_rate
60 0.049 0.064 0.300
120 0.046 0.052 0.425
Show the code 
ggplot(mc_tbl, aes(factor(calibration_n), improvement_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = cores_smf[["primaria"]], width = .5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = fmt(100 * improvement_rate, 0)), vjust = -0.4) +
  labs(x = "rows in the calibration partition", y = "ECE improvement rate (%)",
       title = "Calibration improves only with enough data") +
  ylim(0, 1)

4 Thresholds: turning probability into decision

The 0.5 threshold is rarely the right one when classes are imbalanced and errors have different costs. smf_optimize_threshold() sweeps the grid and returns the best threshold for the chosen metric — with the full curve.

Show the code 
best_f1 <- smf_optimize_threshold(disease$disease[i_te], p_te, metric = "f1",
                                  grid = seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.05),
                                  positive_label = "1")
tab_smf(best_f1$curve, caption = "Threshold sweep for F1 on the test partition.")

Show the code 
ggplot(best_f1$curve, aes(threshold, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = cores_smf[["primaria"]], linewidth = .9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_f1$threshold, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = cores_smf[["alerta"]]) +

       title = "Threshold sweep: F1",

                         " (F1 = ", fmt(best_f1$value, 3), ")")) +
  ylim(0, 1)
TipIn your experiment

Before choosing the threshold, write the cost matrix: how much does a false negative (undetected disease) cost against a false positive (unnecessary control)? With a 10:1 cost for false negatives, the optimal threshold falls even further than the F1 one. The package does not choose for you: it measures the curve so the decision is recorded, not improvised.

5 Part 4 exercises

NoteExercise 4.1 — Search budget

Run the random search with budgets 4, 8 and 16 and record the best inner RMSE and the selected configuration. Does the return justify the cost? Where would you stop?

NoteExercise 4.2 — Missing objective

Ask for mae as an objective in a specification that only declares rmse and read the message. Then fix the specification and repeat. Why is failing loudly better than returning an empty archive?

NoteExercise 4.3 — Calibration with little data

Repeat the calibration replicate with 30 rows. Does the improvement rate fall? What minimum number of calibration rows would you require before trusting the calibrator?

NoteExercise 4.4 — Cost-based threshold

Using the sensitivity curve from smf_optimize_threshold(), find the threshold that guarantees sensitivity >= 0.9. How many extra false positives does that cost relative to the 0.5 threshold?

CautionSolutions

4.1. The best inner RMSE improves little after ~8 evaluations in this small space; the marginal gain does not pay the cost. Budget is a design decision, not an algorithmic one.

4.2. The package aborts with TUNING_OBJECTIVE_NOT_IN_METRICS, listing the specification metrics. Failing loudly avoids the worst failure: an empty selection table that looks like a result.

4.3. With 30 rows, the improvement rate is close to 50% (a coin toss). Rule of thumb: the calibration partition needs hundreds of rows for the Platt calibrator to stabilise; below that, prefer not to calibrate and declare the limitation.

4.4. With sensitivity >= 0.9 the threshold drops to the 0.10-0.15 range, sharply raising false positives. The pedagogical point is that the threshold is a cost decision, and it must come with the curve that supports it.

# Hyperparameter tuning without optimism {#sec-tuning}

Two different questions: **which configuration** of the same model is better
(tuning) and **which model** is better (benchmarking). The package separates
the two and requires the decision criterion to be explicit — including in
multi-objective cases.

```{r data-p4}
field <- ler("field_yield")
v <- verdade$field_yield
no_out <- field[!field$plot_id %in% v$outlier_ids, ]

spec_xgb <- smf_experiment_spec(
  task = smf_task_spec("regression", "yield"),
  data = smf_data_spec("yield", c("nitrogen", "potassium", "water", "organic_matter",
                                  "block", "genotype"),
                       id_column = "plot_id", categorical = c("block", "genotype")),
  design = smf_design_spec(id_column = "plot_id"),
  preprocessing = smf_preprocess_spec("median"),
  model = smf_model_spec("boosted_tree", "xgboost",
                         parameters = list(nrounds = 60L, params = list(max_depth = 3L))),
  metrics = list(smf_metric_spec("rmse", "minimize"), smf_metric_spec("mae", "minimize")),
  reproducibility = smf_reproducibility_spec(61L)
)
space <- smf_search_space(nrounds = smf_param_int(30L, 90L),
                          params.max_depth = smf_param_int(2L, 6L))
print(space)
```

Four search strategies, the same space and the same budget per configuration.
The pedagogical point: **the search method is a budget decision, not a
scientific one** — and the inner resample must be identical for comparisons to
make sense.

```{r tuning-methods-p4}
t_grid <- smf_tune(spec_xgb, no_out, space, smf_tuning_spec("grid", budget = 4L,
  inner_resampling = smf_resampling_spec("kfold", n_splits = 3L, seed = 61L),
  objectives = list(smf_metric_spec("rmse", "minimize")), seed = 61L))
t_rand <- smf_tune(spec_xgb, no_out, space, smf_tuning_spec("random", budget = 6L,
  inner_resampling = smf_resampling_spec("kfold", n_splits = 3L, seed = 62L),
  objectives = list(smf_metric_spec("rmse", "minimize"), smf_metric_spec("mae", "minimize")),
  decision_rule = list(type = "weighted_sum", weights = c(rmse = 0.7, mae = 0.3)),
  seed = 62L))
t_race <- smf_tune(spec_xgb, no_out, space, smf_tuning_spec("racing", budget = 6L,
  inner_resampling = smf_resampling_spec("kfold", n_splits = 4L, seed = 63L),
  objectives = list(smf_metric_spec("rmse", "minimize")), seed = 63L,
  parameters = list(min_folds = 2L)))
t_bayes <- smf_tune(spec_xgb, no_out, space, smf_tuning_spec("bayesian", budget = 6L,
  inner_resampling = smf_resampling_spec("kfold", n_splits = 3L, seed = 64L),
  objectives = list(smf_metric_spec("rmse", "minimize")), seed = 64L,
  parameters = list(initial = 3L, candidate_pool = 16L)))

method_tbl <- data.frame(
  method = c("grid", "random", "racing", "bayesian"),
  evaluations = c(nrow(t_grid@archive), nrow(t_rand@archive),
                  nrow(t_race@archive), nrow(t_bayes@archive)),
  best_rmse = c(min(t_grid@archive$rmse, na.rm = TRUE),
                min(t_rand@archive$rmse, na.rm = TRUE),
                min(t_race@archive$rmse, na.rm = TRUE),
                min(t_bayes@archive$rmse, na.rm = TRUE))
)
tab_smf(method_tbl, caption = "Four search strategies in the same space and with the same inner-fold budget.")
```

```{r tuning-selected}
rand_tbl <- t_rand@archive[, c("trial", "nrounds", "params.max_depth", "rmse", "mae")]
sel_tbl <- t_rand@selected[, c("nrounds", "params.max_depth", "rmse", "mae")]
tab_smf(rand_tbl, caption = "Random-search archive: each row is a configuration evaluated on the inner resample.")
tab_smf(sel_tbl, caption = "Selected by the declared compromise rule (weights 0.7 for RMSE and 0.3 for MAE).")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-tuning
#| fig-cap: "The full archive: each point is a configuration; the dashed line marks the best inner mean. Racing eliminates candidates fold by fold."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of RMSE per evaluation for each search method, with the best-value line."
archives <- rbind(
  data.frame(method = "grid", trial = t_grid@archive$trial, rmse = t_grid@archive$rmse),
  data.frame(method = "random", trial = t_rand@archive$trial, rmse = t_rand@archive$rmse),
  data.frame(method = "racing", trial = t_race@archive$trial, rmse = t_race@archive$rmse),
  data.frame(method = "bayesian", trial = t_bayes@archive$trial, rmse = t_bayes@archive$rmse)
)
ggplot(archives, aes(trial, rmse, colour = method)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = .8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = min(archives$rmse, na.rm = TRUE), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = cores_smf[["alerta"]]) +
  facet_wrap(~method, nrow = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(grid = cores_smf[["neutro"]], random = cores_smf[["primaria"]],
                                 racing = cores_smf[["destaque"]], bayesian = cores_smf[["sucesso"]]),
                      guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "evaluation", y = "inner RMSE (kg/ha)",
       title = "Tuning archives: four search strategies")
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Trap
An objective that is **not** in `spec@metrics` does not produce an empty
archive: it aborts with a clear error (`TUNING_OBJECTIVE_NOT_IN_METRICS`),
listing the available metrics. This behaviour is the 1.0.2 fix for a defect
that returned an empty selection in silence. The package prefers to fail
loudly.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Interpretation
The best inner RMSE across all methods is
`r fmt(min(archives$rmse, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` kg/ha, found by
`r archives$method[which.min(archives$rmse)]`. Inner values are **not** the
final performance: they choose the configuration. The honest estimate of the
chosen one comes from an outer resample (here, the Part 3 holdout; at the
limit, nested tuning).
:::

# Benchmarking: comparing models with a declared criterion {#sec-benchmark}

The benchmark evaluates several **models** in the same design, with
repetitions and computational cost measures. The decision comes from an
explicit rule.

```{r benchmark-p4}
candidates <- list(
  lm = smf_model_spec("linear_regression", "stats"),
  rf = smf_model_spec("random_forest", "tidymodels",
                      parameters = list(model_engine = "ranger")),
  xgb = smf_model_spec("boosted_tree", "xgboost", parameters = list(nrounds = 60L))
)
bench <- smf_benchmark(spec_xgb, no_out, smf_benchmark_spec(
  candidates = candidates,
  metrics = list(smf_metric_spec("rmse", "minimize")),
  resampling = smf_resampling_spec("kfold", n_splits = 5L, seed = 71L),
  compute_measures = c("fit_time", "total_time"),
  repetitions = 2L, seed = 71L
))
tab_smf(bench@summary, caption = "Benchmark with 5 folds repeated twice: mean, SD, standard error and interval per candidate.")
dec <- smf_decide_benchmark(bench, list(type = "weighted_sum", weights = c(rmse = 1)))
tab_smf(dec, caption = "Decision by the declared rule (weight 1 for RMSE).")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-benchmark
#| fig-cap: "Mean performance with confidence interval per candidate: the straight line beats the flexible alternatives on this linear problem."
#| fig-alt: "Point plot with error bars of mean RMSE per candidate."
ggplot(bench@summary, aes(stats::reorder(candidate, mean), mean)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), colour = cores_smf[["primaria"]], size = .8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = fmt(mean, 0)), hjust = -0.35) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "mean RMSE (kg/ha)",
       title = "Benchmark: mean RMSE with interval") +
  ylim(0, max(bench@summary$upper) * 1.15)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Interpretation
The winner by the rule is `r dec$candidate[1]`, with mean RMSE
`r fmt(dec$rmse[1], 1)`. The intervals overlap in part, but the conclusion
does not depend on a single fold: it comes from `r bench@summary$n[1]`
evaluations (5 folds x 2 repetitions) and from a rule declared before looking
at the result.
:::

# Calibration: does the number mean what it promises? {#sec-calibration}

A probability of 0.3 should correspond to ~30% of events. In the disease
dataset, with label noise, that rarely happens without calibration. The
package offers the calibrator (`smf_calibrate()`), the application
(`smf_apply_calibration()`) and the report (`smf_calibration_report()`).

```{r calibration-p4}
disease <- ler("disease_binary")
disease$disease <- factor(disease$disease, levels = c(0, 1))
set.seed(20260919)
idx <- sample.int(nrow(disease))
i_te <- idx[1:100]
i_rest <- idx[101:nrow(disease)]
i_cal <- i_rest[1:120]
i_tr <- setdiff(i_rest, i_cal)
glm_p4 <- stats::glm(disease ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4, data = disease[i_tr, ],
                     family = stats::binomial())
p_cal_tr <- stats::predict(glm_p4, disease[i_cal, ], type = "response")
p_te <- stats::predict(glm_p4, disease[i_te, ], type = "response")
P_te <- cbind(`0` = 1 - p_te, `1` = p_te)
cal_p4 <- smf_calibrate(disease$disease[i_cal],
                        cbind(`0` = 1 - p_cal_tr, `1` = p_cal_tr),
                        smf_calibration_spec("platt"))
P_te_cal <- smf_apply_calibration(cal_p4, P_te)
rel_raw <- smf_calibration_report(disease$disease[i_te], P_te, bins = 5L,
                                  positive_label = "1")
rel_cal <- smf_calibration_report(disease$disease[i_te], P_te_cal, bins = 5L,
                                  positive_label = "1")
cal_tbl <- data.frame(
  measure = c("ECE", "log loss", "Brier"),
  raw = c(rel_raw$ece, rel_raw$log_loss, rel_raw$brier),
  calibrated = c(rel_cal$ece, rel_cal$log_loss, rel_cal$brier)
)
tab_smf(cal_tbl, caption = "Same test set, same logistic regression: before and after Platt calibration (calibration partition: 120 rows).")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-calibration
#| fig-cap: "Reliability curve: predicted probability against observed frequency. The diagonal is perfect calibration."
#| fig-alt: "Reliability points before and after calibration, with a reference diagonal."
conf_raw <- rel_raw$table
conf_raw <- data.frame(predicted = conf_raw$mean_probability,
                       observed = conf_raw$observed_frequency,
                       version = "raw")
conf_cal <- rel_cal$table
conf_cal <- data.frame(predicted = conf_cal$mean_probability,
                       observed = conf_cal$observed_frequency,
                       version = "calibrated")
ggplot(rbind(conf_raw, conf_cal), aes(predicted, observed, colour = version)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  geom_line(alpha = .6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(raw = cores_smf[["neutro"]],
                                 calibrated = cores_smf[["primaria"]])) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "predicted probability (bin mean)", y = "observed frequency",
       colour = NULL,
       title = "Reliability curve: raw vs calibrated") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Interpretation
In this partition, raw ECE is `r fmt(rel_raw$ece, 4)` and calibrated ECE is
`r fmt(rel_cal$ece, 4)`. Calibrating is **not** automatically better: with
only 120 calibration rows, the Platt calibrator can worsen ECE — the effect
depends on the partition size and on noise. The rate below measures the
procedure with repetition, which is the only evidence that decides.
:::

```{r calibration-mc}
one_replicate_cal <- function(s, n_cal) {
  set.seed(s)
  n <- nrow(disease); order_idx <- sample.int(n)
  i_te_r <- order_idx[1:100]
  rest <- order_idx[101:n]
  i_cal_r <- rest[1:n_cal]
  i_tr_r <- setdiff(rest, i_cal_r)
  f <- stats::glm(disease ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4, data = disease[i_tr_r, ],
                  family = stats::binomial())
  p_c <- stats::predict(f, disease[i_cal_r, ], type = "response")
  p_t <- stats::predict(f, disease[i_te_r, ], type = "response")
  Pc <- cbind(`0` = 1 - p_c, `1` = p_c)
  Pt <- cbind(`0` = 1 - p_t, `1` = p_t)
  cr <- smf_calibrate(disease$disease[i_cal_r], Pc, smf_calibration_spec("platt"))
  Ptc <- smf_apply_calibration(cr, Pt)
  r0 <- smf_calibration_report(disease$disease[i_te_r], Pt, bins = 5L, positive_label = "1")
  r1 <- smf_calibration_report(disease$disease[i_te_r], Ptc, bins = 5L, positive_label = "1")
  c(ece_raw = r0$ece, ece_cal = r1$ece)
}
CAL_SIZE <- c(60L, 120L)
R_REP <- 40L
mc_cal <- lapply(CAL_SIZE, function(nc) {
  t(vapply(seq_len(R_REP), function(s) one_replicate_cal(s, nc), numeric(2)))
})
names(mc_cal) <- as.character(CAL_SIZE)
mc_tbl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(CAL_SIZE), function(i) {
  m <- mc_cal[[i]]
  data.frame(calibration_n = CAL_SIZE[i],
             mean_raw_ece = mean(m[, "ece_raw"]),
             mean_calibrated_ece = mean(m[, "ece_cal"]),
             improvement_rate = mean(m[, "ece_cal"] < m[, "ece_raw"]))
}))
tab_smf(mc_tbl, caption = "Platt calibration over 40 independent splits, by calibration partition size.")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-mc-calibration
#| fig-cap: "Calibration improvement depends on partition size: with 60 rows the improvement rate is low; with 120 it rises."
#| fig-alt: "Bars of ECE improvement rate by calibration partition size."
ggplot(mc_tbl, aes(factor(calibration_n), improvement_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = cores_smf[["primaria"]], width = .5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = fmt(100 * improvement_rate, 0)), vjust = -0.4) +
  labs(x = "rows in the calibration partition", y = "ECE improvement rate (%)",
       title = "Calibration improves only with enough data") +
  ylim(0, 1)
```

# Thresholds: turning probability into decision {#sec-thresholds}

The 0.5 threshold is rarely the right one when classes are imbalanced and
errors have different costs. `smf_optimize_threshold()` sweeps the grid and
returns the best threshold for the chosen metric — with the full curve.

```{r thresholds}
best_f1 <- smf_optimize_threshold(disease$disease[i_te], p_te, metric = "f1",
                                  grid = seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.05),
                                  positive_label = "1")
tab_smf(best_f1$curve, caption = "Threshold sweep for F1 on the test partition.")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-threshold
#| fig-cap: "F1 curve against the threshold: the optimum (0.25) is well below the default 0.5 — a consequence of imbalance."
#| fig-alt: "F1 curve against the threshold, with the optimum point marked."
ggplot(best_f1$curve, aes(threshold, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = cores_smf[["primaria"]], linewidth = .9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_f1$threshold, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = cores_smf[["alerta"]]) +
  labs(x = "decision threshold", y = "F1 on the test set",
       title = "Threshold sweep: F1",
       subtitle = paste0("Optimum at ", fmt(best_f1$threshold, 2),
                         " (F1 = ", fmt(best_f1$value, 3), ")")) +
  ylim(0, 1)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## In your experiment
Before choosing the threshold, write the **cost matrix**: how much does a
false negative (undetected disease) cost against a false positive (unnecessary
control)? With a 10:1 cost for false negatives, the optimal threshold falls
even further than the F1 one. The package does not choose for you: it measures
the curve so the decision is recorded, not improvised.
:::

# Part 4 exercises {#sec-exercises-p4}

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise 4.1 — Search budget
Run the random search with budgets 4, 8 and 16 and record the best inner RMSE
and the selected configuration. Does the return justify the cost? Where would
you stop?
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise 4.2 — Missing objective
Ask for `mae` as an objective in a specification that only declares `rmse`
and read the message. Then fix the specification and repeat. Why is failing
loudly better than returning an empty archive?
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise 4.3 — Calibration with little data
Repeat the calibration replicate with 30 rows. Does the improvement rate fall?
What minimum number of calibration rows would you require before trusting the
calibrator?
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise 4.4 — Cost-based threshold
Using the sensitivity curve from `smf_optimize_threshold()`, find the
threshold that guarantees sensitivity >= 0.9. How many extra false positives
does that cost relative to the 0.5 threshold?
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solutions
**4.1.** The best inner RMSE improves little after ~8 evaluations in this
small space; the marginal gain does not pay the cost. Budget is a design
decision, not an algorithmic one.

**4.2.** The package aborts with `TUNING_OBJECTIVE_NOT_IN_METRICS`, listing
the specification metrics. Failing loudly avoids the worst failure: an empty
selection table that looks like a result.

**4.3.** With 30 rows, the improvement rate is close to 50% (a coin toss).
Rule of thumb: the calibration partition needs hundreds of rows for the Platt
calibrator to stabilise; below that, prefer not to calibrate and declare the
limitation.

**4.4.** With sensitivity >= 0.9 the threshold drops to the 0.10-0.15 range,
sharply raising false positives. The pedagogical point is that **the threshold
is a cost decision**, and it must come with the curve that supports it.
:::
